Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Donald Trump Blanche formally rescinds Trump’s $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’ ahead of nomination hearing Todd Blanche issues formal order terminating measure widely derided as a ‘slush fund’, in move that could clear path for his nomination as attorney general Associated Press Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Acting US attorney general Todd Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Donald Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to compensate his political allies, a move that follows weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general. While Blanche has repeatedly said publicly that the fund was dead, the justice department had resisted formally confirming that in writing. That had drawn concern from lawmakers that it could be revived in some form, especially after Trump expressed continued support for the idea. A spokesperson for Texas Senator John Cornyn, one of the senators holding up Blanche’s nomination, confirmed the agreement. The other GOP senator, North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis, did not have immediate comment. The announcement comes ahead of a Senate judiciary committee vote on Blanche, which is scheduled for Tuesday. Trump vows to push $1.8bn slush fund as Senate committee set to reconsider AG nomination Read more “My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche said in a post on X. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order.” The order says that “although the acting attorney general has repeatedly advised Congress through testimony, including under oath, as well as in written responses, that the Fund is not moving forward, and the Department has repeatedly represented to district courts that the Fund is not moving forward, today’s Order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026 Order.” The document released by Blanche on Sunday night also limits the scope of another provision of the settlement that provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits . It clarifies that the tax audit immunity agreement “applies only retroactively” to claims open at the time of the settlement and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings. The two sides have been negotiating for weeks, but Trump has said repeatedly during the talks that he thinks the fund should go forward . Earlier on Sunday evening, Trump said that people who had faced charges from the January 6 attack on the Capitol and could have benefited from the fund had “their lives destroyed”. “This would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered,” Trump said. “A lot of people like it.” Explore more on these topics Donald Trump Trump administration US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Beállítom Új oldalra hívta fel a figyelmet a Tisza Párt alelnöke, Radnai Márk szerint hamarosan indul a Közhang, vagyis Magyarország első közösségi társadalmi egyeztetési platformja. A posztban mutatott logó szerepel azon a még januárban egy magánszemély által regisztrált weboldalon , ahol a következő mondatok váltják egymást: Magyarország első társadalmi egyeztetési platformja. Ne csak nézzük a jövőt, hanem alakítsuk is. Évtizedek óta arra várunk, hogy ne csak ígéretek legyenek. Magyarország jövője közös ügyünk. Hamarosan elindulunk. A Közhang név ismerős lehet, egy régebbi ATV-s műsornak volt ez a címe, amit Juszt László vezetett. Fun fact, hogy ebben a műsorban szerepelt 2002 júniusban a fiatal Magyar Péter, aki a későbbi nézőpontos Mráz Ágoston Sámuellel fejtette meg Medgyessy Péter múltját és az ügynökügyek kezelését. Radnai azt írja a posztban, hogy az oldal indulására „mindannyian várunk”. és az indulással szintet lépnek, hogy együtt írhassák Magyarország jövőjét. Folyamatos társadalmi párbeszédet ígérnek érthető információkkal, edukációval, átláthatósággal és nyomon követhetőséggel, vagyis egyfajta permanens nemzeti konzultáció sejlik fel. A Közhangról a posztban olvashatnak bővebben. Magyar Péter 2026. májusában jelentette be a Működő és Emberséges Magyarország Intézet megalapítását, amelynek keretében – a kormányzati kapcsolattartás biztosítására – Radnai Márkot, a Tisza Párt alelnökét nevezték ki a működő és emberséges Magyarországért felelős kormánybiztosnak. Radnai Márk kormánybiztosként azért felel, hogy „a társadalom véleményét becsatornázza a politikai döntéshozatalba”. Radnai szerint a MEMI egy politikailag független intézmény lesz , „az intézet célja a széles körű társadalmi részvétel megszervezése, amiben nincs pártpolitikai érdek”. Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images Immigration and asylum Number of asylum seekers living in hotels across UK halves in a year Home Office was housing 16,021 asylum seekers across 160 hotels at end of June, while small boat crossings down 23% UK politics live – latest updates Jessica Elgot , Diane Taylor and Chris Osuh Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.31 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The number of asylum seekers living in hotels has halved in a year, Home Office figures show. Sweeping changes to the asylum system have also led to a significant drop in legal arrivals and asylum claims, but the numbers of asylum seekers housed in private accommodation has increased as the government moves people from hotels into privately rented houses in multiple occupation (HMOs). There were 16,021 asylum seekers housed in 160 hotels at the end of June, down from 32,041 at the same point last year and a peak of 56,018 in September 2023. Asylum hotels have been a flashpoint for the far right , especially last summer, and the government has pledged to end their use by the end of the parliament. It said earlier this month another 13 hotels had recently been exited. But tens of thousands of people are still housed in other forms of contingency accommodation, which has also often been highly controversial, both in local communities and because of the conditions of the housing for a vulnerable group of people. The latest figures show 69,038 were housed in temporary accommodation. The shift from asylum hotels to other forms of accommodation has led to an 8% fall in Home Office spending on asylum. The Guardian revealed this month that the government was considering paying higher prices for housing asylum seekers in private rental properties as part of Andy Burnham’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across the country. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood , said figures showed the government was “restoring control at our border and fairness to the migration system”. She said: “A little over two years into office and the asylum backlog is down, the number of asylum seekers in hotels is falling, illegal working arrests are at record levels and deportations and returns are up markedly.” Small boat crossings to the UK have fallen by 23% year on year, which Home Office officials said was down to a combination of more trafficking arrests and more interceptions by French police. View image in fullscreen A counter-protest near an anti-immigration rally in Maidstone, Kent earlier this month. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images The previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, struck a deal with the French government to deport some would-be migrants back to France in exchange for providing others with a safe and legal route to the UK, known as the one in, one out policy. However, Home Office figures show the introduction of the scheme has led to a rise in incidents of use of force against deportees to a record 210, including 181 occasions where restraint equipment was used, a figure that has doubled since the start of the French scheme. Charities say they have documented injuries sustained by asylum seekers as they are removed back to France. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Mahmood said there was still more to do to deter small boat Channel crossings. “Small boats numbers are now falling but we are not complacent and there is more we must do,” she said. “That is why I have boosted enforcement on the French beaches and overseas and introduced new legislation to tackle the pull factors that draw people here through unsafe and illegal routes.” From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons Read more Nuni Jorgensen, of the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory, told PA the government had been able to close hotels largely because asylum decisions were being made more quickly, but there was now an asylum appeals backlog in the courts. Figures also show that the number of businesses being stripped of the right to sponsor migrant workers has surged to the highest since the post-Brexit scheme was introduced. Analysis of quarterly migration statistics and a freedom of information request by the workplace justice charity the Work Rights Centre found the number of revocations of licences to sponsor migrant workers surged to 4,403 in the 12 months to June 2026, from 1,828 in 2025. The skilled worker visa sponsorship scheme was introduced to fill post-Brexit skills shortages in sectors such as care. Unions and charities have warned that the scheme facilitates exploitation. In some cases, workers have complained of employers using the fact that their migration status is tied to their job to underpay them and force them to work long hours. Other arrivals, such as Shabin Shaji , whose case the Guardian reported on earlier this year, paid cash to recruiters to secure a role in the UK but have been left destitute after their employer “ghosted” them. https://www.dw.com/en/serbia-votes-in-cl.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OdWU Voters cast their ballots at a polling station in Belgrade in Serbia's closely contested parliamentary election Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS Advertisement Voting began in Serbia on Sunday in a closely contested election that could bring an end to more than a decade of rule by long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). Polls suggest a tight race between the SNS and the newly formed, youth-backed Students' List. The party emerged from a mass student protest movement sparked by the deadly collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi ‌Sad in 2024. The disaster killed 16 people and stirred widespread anger over alleged corruption, poor construction standards and a lack of accountability for public infrastructure projects. Protesters accused the government of allowing corruption and political patronage to undermine public safety, allegations the authorities have rejected. Demonstrations demanding accountability have since snowballed into Serbia's largest movement since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What began with university students staging blockades and marches soon drew support from teachers, farmers and other sections of Serbian society, turning a demand for justice over the disaster into a broader challenge to Vucic's grip on power. Vucic faces tough election challenge After calling snap elections last month, Vucic stepped down as president to run for prime minister. Under Serbia's constitution, Vucic cannot run for a third presidential term Image: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia's constitution prevents him from serving a third term. Vucic first came to power as prime minister in 2014 before becoming president in 2017. Critics have accused him of concentrating power, undermining independent media and weakening democratic institutions. He and his party deny the allegations. The student movement has sought to channel the energy of the street protests into an electoral challenge, presenting itself as an alternative to both the ruling party and Serbia's established opposition. The election is also being closely watched in Europe. Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership, but its accession process has been hampered by concerns over democratic standards and the rule of law. Vucic has also maintained close ties with Russia and refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The vote comes six months after Peter Magyar's victory in Hungary , when he defeated Vucic's ally, Viktor Orban . Polling stations close at 8 p.m. local time (1900 GMT).
